name: Glaciermere
description: Glaciermere is a splinter of a world, small enough to cross on foot in a long season, its face polished by eons of vacuum into fields of mirror-bright ice. A single vast impact crater—the Mere itself—dominates the near hemisphere, its floor glazed with impact glass that catches starlight like a frozen eye. With no atmosphere to scatter the light, every shadow is black as a closed door and every star burns hard and unwavering.

To stand here is to stand inside silence. The regolith crunches with a sound that carries through suit gloves and boots alike, and beyond it nothing: no wind, no whisper, no horizon haze. The only warmth is the sunward side of your own visor. Visitors report a strange vertigo, the sense of being balanced on the thinnest skin drawn over an immense dark depth.

That depth is real. Radar soundings revealed a saline ocean trapped beneath twelve kilometers of ice, warmed by radioactive decay in the tiny world's dense core, and sealed within it live the last microbial colonies of a biosphere nearly out of time. The crater that named the planet struck three hundred million years ago and came within a hair of sterilizing the sea entirely; the colonies have never recovered their old range. Then, during a routine gravity survey, instruments recorded a repeating pulse rising from beneath the ice—too regular to be geology, too faint to be anything obvious.

Salvage interests circle Glaciermere for its lodes of exotic matter crystallized in the ancient impact zone, but every survey drone sent toward the signal's source has failed in identical, unnerving ways. Xenobiologists warn that the fragile ocean biosphere could be extinguished by a single carelessly drilled borehole. The race is on between those who want to listen, those who want to mine, and something below that has already begun, very slowly, to answer.
